title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives and Runbooks
author: Nina Patel
body:
Overview:

This document defines Redwood Inference SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning practices, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and runbook structure. It is intended for on-call engineers, SRE owners, product stakeholders, and platform teams who operate inference services (hosted API, dedicated, and private deployments).

Scope and ownership:

- Applies to platform-facing services owned by eng-sre and product-facing teams: inference-api, router-service, batch-inference, kv-cache, embeddings-service, and model-loader.
- Primary owner: eng-sre (SRE team) for cross-service standards; individual services retain SLO ownership and measurement responsibility.
- Exceptions must be documented in the service's ADR and approved by SRE leads.

SLOs and Error Budgets (policy summary):

- Purpose: Provide a measurable contract between SRE/product and consumers; drive prioritization of reliability work using error budgets.
- SLO window: 30-day rolling window for production SLOs unless otherwise noted. Critical cross-region SLAs (enterprise customers) may use 90-day windows as part of contract negotiations.
- SLO vs SLA: SLO is an internal reliability target. SLA (customer-facing) is a legal contract and requires engagement with legal and finance.

SLO definitions (examples for inference-api):

1) Availability SLO (control-plane and data-plane):
   - Metric: successful request ratio (2xx responses for API routes excluding expected 4xx).
   - Target: 99.95% availability over a 30-day rolling window for hosted inference-api (gold tier).
   - Owner: inference-api service owner.

2) Latency SLO (user-facing gen endpoint):
   - Metric: p99 end-to-end response latency for generation requests with prompt length <= 1024 tokens.
   - Target: p99 < 350ms for regional hosted requests; p95 < 150ms.
   - Notes: For long-context workloads (>1024 tokens) use separate SLOs and higher latency thresholds.

3) Embeddings SLO:
   - Metric: p99 latency for embedding requests under 512 tokens.
   - Target: p99 < 120ms, availability 99.9%

SLO measurement & tooling:

- Measurement source: production telemetry pipeline (prometheus + remote write into metrics warehouse). SLOs are computed from a canonical metrics namespace: reddo.slo.<service>.<metric>.
- Burn rate calculation: standard burn rate = (observed_error_rate / (1 - target_slo)) scaled to the evaluation window per RFC.
- Dashboards: per-service SLO dashboards in Grafana with 30d window, error budget burn rate panels, and top contributing error classes.

Error budget policy and automated actions:

- Burn rate thresholds and actions:

  | Burn rate (30m) | Action |
  |-----------------|--------|
  | > 4 (high)      | Immediate page to on-call; convene mitigation bridge; rate limit non-essential traffic; enable feature gates; stop risky rollouts. |
  | 1.5 - 4 (elevated) | Notify owners + SRE runbook execution; pause non-critical deploys; increase tracing sampling; run targeted rollback if root cause indicates release. |
  | 0.5 - 1.5 (watch) | Monitor closely; SRE review within current shift; prepare mitigation steps. |
  | < 0.5 (healthy)  | Normal operations; schedule reliability work as capacity allows. |

- When an error budget is exhausted for a service (remaining budget <= 0):
  1) SRE and product owner meet within 24h to agree on immediate mitigations and rollbacks.
  2) Pause all non-critical deploys and feature rollouts for the impacted service.
  3) Prioritize a corrective reliability initiative (RCI) with target completion date.

Capacity planning and provisioning (practical guidance):

- Targets and headroom:
  - Target utilization for GPU-backed inference pools: 60-70% steady-state to absorb variability and cold-starts.
  - Target CPU-backed services: 50-65% average utilization.
  - Spiky workloads (burst) must have autoscale buffers and pre-warmed pools.

- Forecasting process (quarterly):
  1) Collect baseline metrics: request rate (RPS), tokens-per-request, sequence-length distribution, model-mix (quantized vs full).
 2) Business forecasts from product: expected MRR-driven growth, planned campaigns, and new feature launches.
 3) Run capacity simulations using the perf-suite (see eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite) to estimate GPU-hours and tail-latency at target throughput.
  4) Reserve capacity (Dedicated) or plan cloud scaling policies to meet 99.95% uptime at forecasted load + 20% safety buffer.

- Autoscaling & throttling rules:
  - Autoscale by request concurrency and token throughput, not just instance count.
  - Implement queue-based admission control with priority queues for gold/platinum customers.
  - Enforce soft rate-limiting per-API-key and hard global throttles for overload protection.

Reliability initiatives (RIs):

- Quarterly reliability objectives (QROs): define a 90-day initiative aligned to a major SLO or platform weakness (e.g., reduce p99 latency by 25% for 1024-token gen). Each RI must include metrics, owner, milestones, and resources.
- Typical RIs:
  - KV cache warm-up optimization
  - Prefix caching and reuse across short-lived sessions
  - Kernel selection improvements for common model families
  - Autoscaler policy rewrite to use token-aware batching

Incident review standards and postmortems:

- Immediate requirements after an incident (within 48 hours):
  1) Create an incident page with timeline, impact, and actions taken.
  2) Assign incident lead and note on-call rotation.
  3) Collect raw diagnostics: traces, logs, sampling payloads, and metrics.

- Postmortem structure (published within 7 days):
  - Summary and customer impact (who/how many affected)
  - Timeline of events (timestamps in UTC)
  - Root cause analysis (with evidence)
  - Contributing factors and systemic weaknesses
  - Action items (owner + due date) and follow-up plan
  - Error budget impact and whether SLA notifications were required

- Review cadence: weekly incident review meeting for severity >= Sev2; monthly blameless incident roundup for recurring themes.

Operational tooling and observability (required by default):

- Required dashboards:
  - Per-service SLO dashboard (30d, 7d, 1d windows)
  - Error-class breakdown (by route/model/region)
  - Capacity and utilization dashboard (GPU hours, pre-warmed pool size, queue lengths)
  - On-call runbook quick view with top three runbook steps and contact links

- Alerting guidelines:
  - Alerts should be actionable and tied to runbooks. Every alert must list the responsible owner and suggested first actions.
  - Pager thresholds: only severity >= Sev2 should page (burn rate > 4 or sustained p99 > SLO*1.5 for 15m). Lower severities should create tickets.

- Synthetic tests and chaos engineering:
  - Daily synthetic smoke tests for critical endpoints in each region (generate / embeddings endpoints). Failures create high-priority tickets.
  - Quarterly chaos tests on staging and canary-only experiments in prod (rate-limited) to validate fallbacks and autoscaling.

SRE runbook template (required fields):

- Title: short descriptive name
- Service: service id(s)
- Pager criteria: what pages the runbook handles
- Initial triage (top 5 checks):
  1) Check SLO dashboard and burn rate panel
  2) Verify alert details and recent deploys (CI commit and rollout ID)
  3) Check primary logs (router, inference-runtime) for ERROR/CRITICAL classes
  4) Check queue lengths and rate limits (admission control)
  5) Validate whether model or infra change (kernel, quantization) coincided with the window
- Mitigation steps (numbered):
  1) If burn rate > 4: rate-limit non-ESSENTIAL traffic (runbook command: `rbacctl throttle --service inference-api --policy emergency`)
  2) Pause recent rollouts: `kubectl rollout pause deployment/inference-api --namespace=prod` and evaluate commit diff
  3) If GPU OOM or model failure: switch to compatible fallback model variant (e.g., redwood-model-1-quantized) using router-service feature toggle
  4) Elevated tracing: increase sampling for the affected routes and capture full traces for 15m
  5) If degraded latency only: reduce batch window and increase instance count to drain queues
- Communication checklist:
  - Page on-call Slack channel and include a short PSIRT-style header: severity, impact, in-progress mitigations, next-steps, owner.
  - Update status page and customer-facing comms if SLA is impacted.

Example runbook excerpt (inference-api high error-rate):

1) Triage: confirm error class via Grafana -> `errors.by_class` for last 30m.
2) If >50% of errors are 5xx from model-loader, open the model-loader runbook and follow steps therein.
3) If errors are resource-related (OOM, GPU driver): scale pool and fail traffic to dedicated fallbacks.

Operational readiness & review cycles:

- SLO review: quarterly review with product and SRE to adjust targets based on customer expectations and measurement noise.
- Error budget review: monthly SRE meeting to inspect services with low remaining budgets and prioritize RIs.
- Runbook audit: annual audit of all runbooks (owners must confirm correctness).

Appendices:

- Definitions:
  - SLO: Service Level Objective
  - Burn rate: rate at which the error budget is consumed relative to target
  - Sev1/Sev2: severity levels defined in oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process

- Quick references (commands and links):
  - Metrics namespace: reddo.slo.<service>.<metric>
  - Dashboards: Grafana -> SRE -> <service>-slo-30d
  - Runbooks index: confluence/eng-sre/runbooks-index (link local)

Contact and escalation paths:

- Primary SRE on-call: see oncall rota (eng-sre/runbooks -> oncall schedule)
- Pager backup: team lead (eng-sre-sre-lead@redwood.ai)
- Product owner escalation: product-ops@redwood.ai

This document is normative: new services must adopt these standards at service-launch and include a signed SLO ownership entry in the service README. Exceptions require SRE lead approval and documented compensating controls.
